newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin set to speak on radio about army, economy.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin set to speak on radio about army, economy.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin makes an address to the nation on Friday in which he is expected to speak of the problems facing Russia's armed forces amid mounting speculation he will sack his defence minister.

In his second radio address since recovering from a bout of pneumonia, Yeltsin will also try to demonstrate he is firmly back in control and has a clear idea of what must be done to tackle Russia's deep-seated economic and social ills.

Ekho Moskvy radio said Yeltsin would touch on the 1997 budget, which he signed into law this week. The budget is a central pillar of the government's plans to win vital international funding for its painful market reforms.

This week Yeltsin criticised the government for failing to end delays in the payment of wages and pensions and he told Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to sack some ministers to help defuse social tensions.

Underlining the growing restiveness of Russians, the Federation of Independent Trade Unions said on Thursday it would stage a one-day national strike on March 27 to protest against wage arrears and government social policies.

As speculation raged about next week's cabinet reshuffle, Gennady Seleznyov, communist chairman of the State Duma lower house of parliament, said Yeltsin might dismiss the whole cabinet, including his loyal ally Chernomyrdin.

NTV commercial television quoted Seleznyov as saying Chernomyrdin's most likely successor would be either Yegor Stroyev, head of the upper chamber Federation Council, or Yury Luzhkov, mayor of Moscow.
But most commentators expect the stolid Chernomyrdin, widely viewed as a guarantor of reforms, to survive the shake-up.
Speculation has focused instead on Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, whom Yeltsin rapped this week for "whining" about the state of Russia's demoralised, cash-strapped armed forces.
Yeltsin's meeting on Thursday with a high-flying army general hastily summoned from Russia's Far East helped fuel talk that Rodionov, 60, might be on the way out.
Giving the rumour-mill a further turn, Mayak radio reported that Rodionov had cancelled a trip to Armenia scheduled for next week, just before the government changes are to be announced.
The radio did not say why Rodionov's trip had been called off and the Defence Ministry declined to comment on the report.
Yeltsin's talks with General Viktor Chechevatov, commander of the Far East military district, focused on military reforms.
The general denied he had been offered any new post but said reforms were urgently needed to avert disaster in the army.

"I told the president the troops are controllable and capable of functioning at the moment, but the situation is serious, as in Stalingrad," Chechevatov told Interfax news agency, referring to one of the fiercest battles of World War Two in which one million people died.
Despite the press rumours, Rodionov's dismissal is far from certain. Yeltsin appeared to back him last week and risks more upheaval in the armed forces if he replaces him.
On Thursday, Rodionov sounded a loyal note, telling a group of senior businessmen he fully backed the president's call for military reforms.
"It is time to stop the lamentations and push on with reforms," Interfax quoted him as saying.

In a further sign of Yeltsin's return to active political life after his long illness, the Kremlin boss spoke by telephone on Thursday with U.S. President Bill Clinton about their summit in Helsinki, set for March 20-21.
Topping the summit's agenda will be NATO plans to expand eastwards to include former Warsaw Pact countries.
Moscow fiercely opposes the plans, saying they threaten its own security, but Yeltsin has said he is optimistic he can reach a compromise with Clinton in Helsinki.
